before.text:
ABSTRACT. We outline a proof that if the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
         holds, then every odd number above 5 is a sum of three prime numbers. The
         proof involves an asymptotic theorem covering all but a finite number of cases,
         an intermediate lemma, and an extensive computation.

unit_result_entry.title: Search near the interval endpoint and precompute the small difference primes
unit_result_entry.why_material: The optimized approach reverses which prime set is expensive: it takes consecutive primes near the interval start, precomputes odd primes only up to roughly the interval width, and covers targets by translated copies of that fixed small-prime set. A density calculation motivates a finite candidate count without serving as the certification itself.

unit_dependency_entry.context_note: The span includes the new recurrence, fixed interval width, size estimate, and heuristic explaining the choice of candidate count.
unit_dependency_entry.representation_dependency: Set symbols and superscripts are degraded, and the density calculation is heuristic; the algorithmic reversal is explicit in prose.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Conventional Goldbach verification as cumulative translated-set coverage
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: The usual computation builds primes in a target interval and cumulatively unions their translations by small odd primes until every even target is covered. The passage isolates prime generation as the bottleneck and records how the auxiliary interval margin depends on the largest small prime used.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: The optimized covering method trades one reusable sieve for cheap per-interval prime discovery
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: The paper directly compares resource profiles: the older method sieves all primes in every high interval, while the new method sieves a larger low prime table once and then locates only a bounded list of primes near each interval. It also states the semantic cost: the witness prime is not extremal.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: Reframing witness search as cumulative coverage by translated prime sets exposes a data-layout choice: precompute the reusable small-difference primes, cheaply generate a few high primes per interval, and realize each translation as a bitset shift and OR.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The density argument only motivates the candidate count; completeness comes from actual interval coverage, and primality generation depends on the quoted bounded-base result.
related_synthesis_entries.title: Goldbach verification as translated-set coverage

before.text:
In the first approach, a small set of small primes up to 5000, say, has to be
available, and for each interval [a, b] to be treated, all the primes in [a, b] have to be
generated. In the second approach, a large set of small primes up to about 108 +10 4
has to be generated (only once), and for each interval (a, b] to be treated, one has to
find the largest k primes ::::; a. Of course, this is much cheaper than to find all the
primes in the interval [a, b]. The price to pay is that for each e E [a, b] some prime
p is found for which e - p is prime, but in general this p is neither the smallest nor
the largest such prime.
